name: Verifying What a Model Produced
title: Verifying What a Model Produced
answer: Verifying what a model produced means checking the output of an AI system against the purpose it was meant to serve, the sources it relied on, and the rules that apply to its use. It covers generated text, code, images, predictions, summaries, and recommendations, not just the model itself. This work sits in governance and fiduciary risk because a person or institution acting on unverified output can harm clients, customers, patients, or markets. It is separate from model training and from benchmark evaluation, though it uses both as inputs.

sections.body: Verifying what a model produced means checking the output of an AI system against the purpose it was meant to serve, the sources it relied on, and the rules that apply to its use. It covers generated text, code, images, predictions, summaries, and recommendations, not just the model itself. This work sits in governance and fiduciary risk because a person or institution acting on unverified output can harm clients, customers, patients, or markets. It is separate from model training and from benchmark evaluation, though it uses both as inputs.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on logging and lineage systems that record which model version, data, prompt, and parameters produced an output. It also needs model registries, data catalogs, version control, access controls, and storage that keeps an audit trail. Automated checks run in evaluation harnesses and test suites, while human review queues and case management tools handle exceptions. Dashboards and alerting show failure rates, drift, and unresolved findings over time.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A team starts by defining acceptance criteria for the output, such as factual accuracy, citation quality, policy compliance, and fitness for the intended decision. It then samples outputs, compares them with trusted sources or ground truth, and runs automated tests for consistency, safety, and security. Domain experts review the cases that matter most, and they document what they found, what failed, and what changed. For generative systems, this often includes fact checking, source tracing, adversarial testing, and checks for bias or hallucination. The results feed back into prompts, retrieval sources, model versions, and review thresholds.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on who is accountable for the output, what evidence is kept, and who can inspect it. Provenance records should show the model, data, and human edits behind a result, along with retention and disclosure rules. Privacy, intellectual property, bias, security, and contractual duties all shape what verification must cover. Fiduciary risk adds a duty of care and loyalty, so the institution must be able to explain how it checked the output and why it trusted it. Verification does not remove risk, it makes the remaining risk visible and assignable.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Verification is moving from periodic review toward continuous monitoring, with automated checks running alongside model deployment. Provenance standards, watermarking, and digital signatures are becoming more common for generated content. Third party audits, model attestation, and insurance products are growing around high stakes uses. AI agents that take actions will need verification of both the output and the action, including permissions, logs, and rollback paths. The direction is toward verification as a documented control, not a one time test.
